title: Vend-A-Shoe
oneLine: I built a physical shoe vending machine where a Next.js web app writes a command, a Raspberry Pi worker polls roughly every 1 s, and 4 MG996R servos dispense the selected shoe.
overview: Vend-A-Shoe exists because the client needed a real unit, not a bench demo. The architecture is browser command -> Supabase queue -> Pi worker -> GPIO/PWM -> physical dispense. I integrated the enclosure, harness, power distribution, and control software so that path stayed reliable with 4 servos, 8 LEDs, and a fan in the same box. Early failures looked like software bugs; many were actually electrical and mechanical issues, including faulty servos and power mistakes. The useful debugging loop was isolating one layer at a time with a known-good actuator, a bench supply, and a meter before touching code.
keyHighlights: Built the cloud-to-hardware command path: Next.js UI insert, Supabase queue row, Pi worker poll/claim loop, then servo PWM actuation
Integrated 4 MG996R servos, 8 LEDs, and a fan with shared grounding and separate high-current planning so actuator load did not collapse the control path
Used structured fault isolation to separate software issues from faulty servos, rail problems, and packaging constraints during bring-up
architecture: Dashboard inserts bin commands into Supabase.
Pi worker claims, actuates, writes completed or failed.
Protoboard distributes servo, LED, and fan power with a common ground.
UI writes command rows into `device_commands` through Supabase client.
Pi worker polls oldest `pending` command, claims atomically by status transition, executes servo script, then marks `completed` or `failed`.
`supabase.sql` defines queue table, status indexes, and permissive MVP RLS policies for select/insert/update.
Servo script performs PWM sweep from home duty to target duty and returns home; supports per-bin duty overrides.
Systemd unit keeps worker process alive on boot with restart semantics and environment-based credentials.
challenges: Fitting 4 servos, 8 LEDs, a fan, harness, Pi, and power conversion into a serviceable enclosure.
Protecting logic behavior while servos pulled high current during movement peaks.
Managing 40+ wires without losing rework access or introducing branch faults.
Distinguishing software bugs from dead servos, rail sag, and mechanical drag.
Keeping backend behavior compatible with an existing frontend contract.
lessonsLearned: The biggest skill was debugging across systems, not inside any one of them.
Power supply and multimeter measurements beat intuition when rails sag and grounds float.
Breadboard success does not survive transport.
Packaging and power decide whether the software loop looks correct in the field.
Mechanical variance forces software-level calibration hooks.
State transitions make hardware workflows debuggable when remote.
technicalNotes: Decision: queue-based cloud-to-device architecture through Supabase
Why: avoids exposing Raspberry Pi directly to internet; keeps command history durable.
Tradeoff: introduces polling delay and status reconciliation complexity.
Why: gives observability and recovery semantics for physical actions.
Tradeoff: requires extra state management in worker and UI.
Decision: per-bin GPIO mapping + optional per-bin duty-cycle override
Why: bins have different mechanical behavior; one motion profile was not enough.
Tradeoff: calibration overhead increases as hardware lanes grow.
Worker deployment uses systemd with restart-on-failure and explicit env variables.
nextImprovements: Custom KiCad distribution PCB with keyed connectors and branch fusing/PTCs
Incoming actuator burn-in plus closed-loop dispense sensing
Static DHCP reservation / mDNS and stronger queue auth beyond MVP

debuggingNotes: Bin 3 over-rotation was fixed with per-bin duty calibration instead of one global motion profile.
Quiet channels were tested by swapping known-good servos and known-good GPIO lanes before rewriting worker logic.
A power-side mistake damaged actuators; recovery required replacing hardware and validating each rail under load before resuming integration.
finalOutcome: Working unit shipped to the client after breadboard bring-up, protoboard permanence, wall power, and multi-bin calibration.
